content: Diarrhoeal diseases are a leading cause of mortality among children, claiming millions of lives annually. Flies are well-established vectors for transmitting infectious diarrhoea, yet fly control is rarely emphasized as a preventive strategy. Theoretically, reducing diarrhoea through fly control can be achieved by targeting four key areas: eliminating or reducing fly breeding sites, minimizing sources that attract flies, preventing flies from coming into contact with pathogens, and protecting individuals, food, and utensils from fly contamination. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of various fly control measures in reducing the incidence, morbidity, and mortality associated with diarrhoea in children under five years of age. To achieve this, a comprehensive search of electronic databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, and LILACS, was conducted up to May 24, 2018. Additional searches included trial registries for grey literature and ongoing studies, as well as reference lists of identified studies and reviews. No restrictions were applied regarding language, publication status, or date. The inclusion criteria for the review encompassed randomized controlled trials (RCTs), quasi-RCTs, and controlled before-and-after studies that investigated the impact of fly control interventions on diarrhoea in children under five. Data extraction and risk of bias assessment were independently performed by two reviewers. When necessary, study authors were contacted for additional information. The certainty of the evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. The review included one cluster-RCT conducted in Pakistan, involving 491 participants. This trial assessed the impact of insecticide spraying during the first two years and baited fly traps in the third year. Insecticide spraying was found to reduce the fly population during the four months of the year when flies and diarrhoea cases were most prevalent. This reduction in fly numbers was associated with a decrease in diarrhoea incidence during the first year (mean episodes per child-year: 6.3 in the intervention group vs. 7.1 in the control group) and the second year (mean episodes per child-year: 4.4 in the intervention group vs. 6.5 in the control group; rate ratio [RaR] 0.77, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.67 to 0.89, low-certainty evidence). However, in the third year, the use of baited fly traps did not significantly affect the fly population or diarrhoea incidence (RaR 1.15, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.47, low-certainty evidence). The authors concluded that insecticide spraying may reduce diarrhoea in children in settings with clear seasonal peaks in fly populations and diarrhoea cases. However, further research is needed to determine whether these findings are generalizable to other settings. Additionally, further studies are required to evaluate the effects, feasibility, costs, and acceptability of other fly control methods.
